speechtext:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCIDENCE OF SUICIDE AS CAUSE OF DEATH
speechtext:
Among adult Canadians the incidence of suicides ranks third as a cause of death. For example in 1964, within the 15 to 29 year age group there were 2,482 deaths due to accidents; 402 deaths due to cancer and 269 deaths due to suicide.

Although studies are not at the present time being conducted the department is actively engaged in collecting information on the causes and prevention of suicides and on other mental and behavioral disorders. A number of research projects aimed at a greater understanding and control of depression and anxiety are being supported through the Public Health Research Grants Program.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I wish to submit five reasons for urgency of debate. The first reason I submit is that there will be no further opportunity during this session to debate the matter. The estimates of the minister are passed, there are no more supply motions and therefore there will not be any other opportunity in my judgment to have such debate.
The second reason for urgency is because the Economic Council no more than two days ago issued a report warning of the dangers of a rapidly intensifying housing shortage. Knowing the restrained language of the council this means that we already have a housing problem of major and massive proportions. Every week end hon. members are inundated with telephone calls from people pleading for places in which to live at prices they can afford. But there are none.
A further need for urgency arises from the fact that since the Economic Council of Canada obtains most of its information from government sources, the government has itself known all along about this difficult situation, but has ignored it completely and failed to act.

speechtext: We are considering the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1967. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, vote No. 1, is to be found at page 52 of the blue book.
1. Grant in respect of the net operating amount required to discharge the responsibilities of the national broadcasting service, $110,643,000.

November 23, 1966
Supply-C.B.C.

Mr. Chairman, I am prompted to rise at this time during our consideration of the hon. lady's estimates because of a statement I made on March 9, 1966 which is to be found at page 2459 of Hansard for that day. At that time I said in part.
Before the estimates of the C.B.C. come before us next time, I want to say that I am going to move a motion that they be reduced to one dollar.
I intend to move such a motion later this day.
Before I go into the subject I wish to discuss, service to the remote areas of Canada, let me point out the weakness of dealing with estimates in this manner. The government house leader said earlier today that dealing with estimates is one of the most important pieces of business we can perform in this house. The people of Canada know that one of the prime responsibilities of the opposition is to scrutinize these estimates in a very meticulous manner. Under the new provisional rules we are not able to do that.
At a meeting yesterday of the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts I attempted to put my position to the officials of the C.B.C. I see those officials now sitting in the gallery and I apologize to them because they will have to sit and listen to me say the same things over again. This is a very important matter.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I was in the house last night until the adjournment motion and I heard the introduction of the order proposed by the Minister of Public Works. He is recorded in Hansard at pages 10223 and 10224 as having said:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder, before you call the adjournment motion, if I might deal with one matter. Pursuant to the provisions of the provisional standing order dealing with consideration of supply and estimates, the house leaders have discussed the requirements of that order and we have reached a consensus. I move:
"That on Friday, November 25, 1966, at 5.30 p.m., every question necessary to dispose of all outstanding main and supplementary estimates tabled in this session, and thereafter all subsequent proceedings leading to the passage of the appropriation bill based thereon shall be forthwith disposed of without amendment or debate, notwithstanding the provisions of any standing order."
I should like to ask the house leader whether the estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are now being withdrawn from the committee of which the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek and I are members? That committee is at present discussing these estimates and at 9.30 tomorrow morning
[The Chairman.]
the general manager and president of the C.B.C. are to appear. Are these estimates to be withdrawn without any notice to the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I shall be glad to answer the question. As far as I know the broadcasting committee at the moment has no business before it. A motion referring estimates to a standing committee always takes the form of referring certain estimates saving always the right of the committee of supply to consider them. These estimates were withdrawn by the motion of last night but even without that withdrawal they could be dealt with here. It is still my view that they are not now before the committee although I hesitate to give a legal opinion on a subject of this kind. Let me hasten to add that there is a motion on the order paper to refer the white paper on broadcasting to that committee. When that motion has been dealt with the committee will be able to carry on its work in an uninterrupted way. That committee will have full authority, beyond any shadow of doubt, to carry on a full examination into the affairs of the C.B.C. and the B.B.G. Whenever this house makes that reference to the committee it will be in a position to carry out that examination.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that the estimates of the C.B.C. have been withdrawn from the committee by any action taken last night. If that were so why would the second paragraph of the order passed last night indicate that the matter has to be voted on at 5.30 on Friday? It reads as follows:
2. In the event that any items of these estimates are unreported by any standing committee, such items shall be deemed to have been reported by such standing committee and to stand referred to the committee of supply, and any motion referring such items to any such committee shall be rescinded and the order discharged.
I intended to question the president and general manager of the C.B.C. at the meeting of the broadcasting committee tomorrow. I cannot do it in the House of Commons. The committee met on Thursday of last week and on Tuesday of this week. Tomorrow it is to meet again. I do not believe the estimates of the C.B.C. should be discussed at this time because they have not been withdrawn from the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I could not agree more with the hon. member for York-Humber and I would like to endorse his remarks with regard to the method in which
November 23, 1966

business is carried on in the house. I had hoped to receive some answers from the president of the C.B.C. to questions which I put to him yesterday. I say again that the provisional rules under which we are working at the present time make a mockery of our efforts to get to the bottom of situations which we wish to discuss in detail in committee because, as has been said in the house today, on Friday the guillotine will fall on all estimates regardless of whether or not they are now being considered in a committee. I am sure there are many others like me who would like to speak not only on the estimates of the C.B.C. but on the estimates of other departments which have not been passed by the house. The reason I rise at this time is that I firmly believe that the C.B.C. is not carrying out the intention of parliament.
Mr. Chairman, I have one more question. Will you make a ruling on whether the C.B.C. estimates are before the committee of supply at this time?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is difficult for the chairman to make a ruling on something that has been agreed to by the different parties in the house. It is my understanding that the motion was made an order of the house last evening and was agreed to. It was said by the Minister of Public Works that it was agreed that the estimates would be withdrawn from the standing committees and again referred to the committee of supply on the passing of this motion. If my understanding is not correct, I will have to refer the hon. member to the statement made by the minister.
The Minister of Public Works stated that he was not too certain and that he could not give a legal opinion on the question I raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I only said that about the last of the several points raised by the hon. member. It is clear that the estimates have been returned to the committee of supply. What the hon. member referred to as being said by me dealt with the latter part of his argument.

I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that it is anticipated the standing committee on broadcasting will very shortly be charged with another item of business, the white paper on broadcasting, a motion to this effect having been on the order paper for some time. At that time my hon. friends will have full opportunity to recall any witnesses they choose
Supply-C.B.C.
and to continue the questioning they have started.

Mr. Chairman, we may be dealing with the white paper at some future date in the committee on broadcasting but the withdrawal of the estimates fom the committee at this time will prevent us from getting a breakdown of the vote, which is my present concern. I point out to the house that the information contained in the blue book in regard to the C.B.C. is very vague and means very little to most of us who are on the committee if we are not given the opportunity to ask some questions of the officials. It is said about vote 1 on page 53:
Grant in respect of the net operating amount required to discharge the responsibilities of the national broadcasting service.
I do not think for one moment that anyone in the house or any Canadian, with the exception of those who are in the C.B.C., knows what those responsibilities are. In my attempt to find out what they are I referred to back issues of Hansard to discover what was said at the time the C.B.C. was first established.
I should like to do what I did yesterday in committee, namely, ask questions in regard to vote 1. My first question is: What are the responsibilities of the national broadcasting service? I do not think the minister can answer this question, for reasons which I will state later.
The second question which I should like to ask the president of the C.B.C. is whether a list of priorities has been established or ever been made known to parliament or to the Canadian public. As I said before, I do not believe the C.B.C. or its officials are carrying out the intent of parliament, particularly with regard to people in remote areas where it appears that the C.B.C. is only giving lip service to the initial responsibilities with which it was charged.
I have tried to study the white paper on broadcasting to which the minister referred a few moments ago. On page 15 of the white paper there appears a section entitled: "The Mandate Of The Corporation". I will read the first paragraph of that section:
Under the present Broadcasting Act, responsibility is assigned to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the operation of a national broadcasting service. The interpretation of this phrase has been left largely to the corporation itself-
I think the word "largely" should be changed to "solely". It continues further:
-and it has fulfilled its prime responsibility to provide broadcasting services to the Canadian

November 23, 1966
Supply-C.B.C.
people as a whole in a manner that is altogether praiseworthy.
What really concerns me is the word "fulfilled". Possibly I should not refer to another debate which took place in the house but I should like to mention that in the discussion on a defence issue not long ago reference was made to the white paper on defence and the term "united services" was used. That is a very broad term which can mean anything but to me it certainly does not mean unification. I have the same doubts about the word "fulfilled" which is used in this paragraph.
I wish to draw the minister's attention to the 1965 report of the committee on broadcasting where the following statement appears:
The most pressing need, that which deserves priority in the plans for expansion of the Canadian radio-television system, is the extension of service to all those parts of Canada which have none.
Furthermore, on page 126 of the Fowler report the following recommendation is made:
We recommend:
That the mandate of the public broadcasting agency should be clearly stated and defined as fully as possible by legislation, and should be expanded and specifically explained in a white paper on broadcasting policy.
This recommendation of the Fowler commission does not appear in the white paper on broadcasting. It is stated in the white paper that the minister to whom the C.B.C. is responsible should define the responsibilities of the corporation. These responsibilities are not defined in the white paper nor can they be found anywhere else. I wonder what this large sum of money comprises. We cannot get a breakdown of the $108 million. I believe the minister will agree with me that if that sum is broken down in relation to the number of homes in Canada we will find that about 4.5 million homes are each paying roughly $20 a year to the C.B.C. What are they getting in return? I am speaking for those people who live in remote areas of Canada and who are not getting the services of the C.B.C. which they were initially supposed to receive.
I would also like to refer to what the minister has said on former occasions in the house and particularly in March of this year. On March 8 of this year the minister said, as found on page 2418 of Hansard:
-the question of the extension of the services provided by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, first of all to parts of Canada not yet reached by any service. I fully agree, as I am sure every hon. member does, that it should be extended to such regions as quickly as is humanly possible, if it is humanly possible.

[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
As far as I am concerned those last words have only got me into a lot of trouble in my constituency. My constituency covers a large area of southwest Saskatchewan where it is humanly possible to service these people. Although there may only be a few members of the house who have the same problems I have with C.B.C. service to remote areas, I assure the house that the problems are serious. The members to whom I refer are not confined to one part of the house; they are members from all parties. I hope that those members who have these problems will support me in the motion I intend to move in a few moments.
I ask those who do not have this problem to consider the fact that their constituents do receive C.B.C. service. The people I am talking about are helping to pay for that service. I suppose it is unconstitutional to allow these people an allowance free of income tax because they do not receive this service, or will not receive it, but it does seem to me very unfair that they should pay $20 a home and can never expect to receive service.
The argument was made yesterday that it is nothing new not to receive service of one kind or another. Reference was made to roads and hospitals in rural areas. However, I suggest this argument does not hold water. These people can have roads if they wish to pay for them and they can also have hospitals. But in the case of C.B.C. service there are government and C.B.C. restrictions which prevent provision of this service so that even if these people wished to pay for it they could not receive it.
I should like to remind the minister of that part of her remarks in which she said service would be provided if humanly possible. I firmly believe that the minister is sincere in this statement. However, I know that her hands are tied under the act, and it was this statement that led me to look at the act.
The minister further said on March 8, as reported at page 2418 of Hansard:
I share with all hon. members who have spoken a desire to see as quickly as practicable the extension of service to every Canadian in Canada who can receive it.
Again I think she is sincere.
At page 2418 of Hansard she is reported as having said:
-I am told that we cannot hope under present technological advances to reach 100 per cent of the homes of Canada.
November 23, 1966



We fully understand that it is technically impossible to provide television service for certain homes which are situated at the top of a mountain or in a valley or in between two mountains or in some area with minerals in the ground preventing the reception of the signal. I do not know the technological problems but I know there are difficulties of reception in certain areas. But I am not referring to such areas. I am referring to areas where it is humanly possible to receive television signals, and provision of service may be just a matter of dollars and cents.
Another hon. member who is going to speak on these estimates will draw to the attention of the committee the fact that we do not believe that the officials of the C.B.C. have been fair in the formula they have used to give priority to remote areas which will be serviced. I will not delve into this argument at this moment because the hon. member for Churchill, who so ably put the position on Hansard before, will repeat his arguments, to which I give my support. The figures used by the C.B.C. to show how much it will cost to give these areas television service are not fair.
I also wish the committee to remember that according to this year's estimates all fiomes in Canada will pay over $26 per home for C.B.C. service. The figures used by the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to show what it will cost to put these satellites, or whatever they are called, into operation vary from $5 to $15. The figure we have been using is $20 a home, and we are dealing with over $100 million. There are about four and a half million homes with an average of four people to each home. So that within two years the cost of a satellite or the extension of some station's service would be paid for.
If it is a question of money, Mr. Chairman, the officials of the corporation certainly have no compunction about coming to parliament and asking for additional money. We have not been able to scrutinize the estimates sufficiently to ask the officials how much it will cost in dollars and cents to do this. The vote is not broken down in any way and I do not see in any summary a breakdown of the figures. This is one of the values of sending these estimates to committee, but under the provisional rules the committee does not work as well as it should. With the shortage of time here it is impossible for us to ask the minister to get this information for us. The officials are not members of the house so we cannot ask them.
Supply-C.B.C.
In previous remarks in the house the minister, to my satisfaction, documented briefly the intent of parliament vis-a-vis the C.B.C. over the past 25 or 30 years that the corporation has been in operation. As reported at page 2454 of Hansard for March 9 she said:
-it is not my place to tell the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation where they should extend service.
She implies that by law it is the responsibility of the corporation to determine priorities. In my view it has not yet determined priorities. However, as I said before, parliament has made known its intention and I believe the original intention of parliament was that the C.B.C. should provide service to all Canadians. Certainly that should be its major priority before extending, and duplicating service in areas already served.
I further suggest that perhaps all parts of Canada should have service before the C.B.C. even enters the field of colour television. We are not objecting to the entry into the field of colour television and keeping up with progress, but for the life of me I cannot understand why the program of the corporation in servicing remote areas has not been more extensive.
According to a recent report of the proceedings of the broadcasting committee the minister said that the most pressing need, that which deserved priority in the plans for expansion of the Canadian radio-television system, is the extension of service to all those parts of Canada which have none. I contend that it was the original intention of parliament that the C.B.C. should service all parts of Canada it is humanly possible to service.
C.B.C. applications for licences in larger centres where there is already an alternative service have unnecessarily delayed extension of service to more remote areas. May I refer to the action of the C.B.C. in Edmonton where private operations already exist. Yet the C.B.C. set up another station. I also refer to the situation in Saskatoon where the station in operation is a C.T.V. affiliate. That area has adequate coverage, at least until the remote areas of the province are given service.
C.B.C. capital expenditure on properties and accommodation in large centres has also delayed unnecessarily the servicing of areas which are entitled to be serviced. After many years of saying that it did not feel justified in requesting a special grant from parliament to complete the job of servicing the remote areas that can be serviced, the C.B.C. has finally in its last two annual reports stated that such a grant would be very helpful.

November 23, 1966
Supply-C.B.C.
My question is: Why has it not requested this special grant? We cannot ask the minister because this vote is not broken down. We do not know what the $108 million is for, whether for salaries, productions or capital expenditures. We do not know whether there is anything in this vote to pay for the servicing of the remote areas to which I have referred. If the corporation has requested a special grant, what has been the attitude of the government toward this request? Has the government refused the C.B.C. a grant for the purpose of servicing remote areas, even if granting the request meant a higher per capita cost in some areas than others? I think we have a right to discuss this subject, and I hope the hon. member for Churchill will say more about this matter with particular reference to what we request the C.B.C. to do.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
On page 123 of the Fowler report, under the heading of "The C.B.C. Mandate", we find one or two statements I wish to quote. The first one is:
-the C.B.C. has the primary responsibility tor providing excellent broadcasting services to the Canadian people.
Another statement is:
As the recipient of large sums of public money, it can do many things that the private broadcasters cannot reasonably be expected to do.
Again, we see this statement:
If the interpretation-
Here they are referring to section 25 of the act:
-has failed to conform to the wishes of parliament, it is clear where the responsibility rests.
I think the responsibility rests with parliament. It may not rest so much on the minister or the government but it is time parliament told the C.B.C. what to do and what is expected. We have asked too few questions in the past about the corporation and it may be necessary-I shall be glad to hear arguments against this-to tell the corporation what we consider to be its priorities.
In the latest version the mandate that the C.B.C. conceives it has received from parliament is in part that Canadians who live in remote or heavily populated areas should be as adequately and equitably served as possible by the national system. I do not believe that the purpose of this vote is to set up the C.B.C. in competition with private enterprise but rather to enable it to service those areas where it is not financially sound for private broadcasters to inaugurate a service. There

may be some argument about that last statement.
My thinking about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is that it ought to provide service to those areas of Canada where it is financially impossible for private broadcasters to operate at a profit. The corporation should operate in the way the post office operates. The post office does not necessarily make a profit. It must give service to all people and I think the people are willing to pay in taxation for any deficit it incurs. The same principle should apply to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. All people, most of all those in remote areas, should have C.B.C. service.
An argument could be made that it is more important to provide C.B.C. service to remote areas than to urban centres because in urban centres there are many other forms of entertainment. In western Canada particularly we want to keep the young people on the farms producing the world's food, and to meet our responsibility to keep these young people on the farm they should be entertained, and the government of Canada should be prepared to pay for it. The people in remote areas are paying in this vote for services to all Canadians, although those services are not extended to remote areas. In my opinion the remote areas should be a primary responsibility before other areas. Certainly the remote areas should be considered before services in other areas are duplicated.
Perhaps I have spoken too long. Before sitting down I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill:
That Vote No. 1 of the estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation be reduced by the sum of $107,942,999.00.

speechtext: The question is on the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, listening to the last speaker reminded me of the popular song, "How can you keep them down on the farm". According to the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, we can do it by providing people with television service. Like the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek I regret the circumstance that has brought these estimates from the broadcasting committee back to the house. We had expected to have another meeting with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation officials tomorrow, having had one yesterday. I know that the committee spent a good deal of time this spring on the C.B.C., but that was on the "Seven Days" controversy in which there was a good deal of interest. I do not think one could have
November 23, 1966

expected the committee to discuss the estimates in detail at that time. I also point out that the committee has not yet discussed the estimates of the Board of Broadcast Governors or of the National Film Board. It seems to me that we should be able to do the work of the house and committees in a better way. Here we are faced with the end of the estimates and the estimates of the B.B.G. and the National Film Board have not been examined.
The house leader and the minister have assured us that the white paper on broadcasting will be referred to the committee. I hope this is very soon. It seems to me that unless it is referred to it in the very near future there will be no value in sending it to the committee. I hope the government will be interested in the recommendations of the committee on the white paper and I imagine that if the government has not already done so it is thinking of preparing legislation. Unless the committee deals with the subject soon, it cannot be of help in that regard.
I had an opportunity to question the president of the corporation in committee yesterday but I had not finished as I yielded to other members who wanted to put questions also. Had we resumed our meetings tomorrow we should have gone into some matters we wanted to raise. I should have liked to hear a progress report on the recommendations made by the broadcasting committee last summer. I should have liked to hear about the recommendations made by Mr. Stuart Keate regarding the administrative structure and the recommendation that vice presidents be appointed to be in charge of production in Toronto and Montreal. I know there is great difficulty in finding the right type of person to fulfil the requirements suggested by Mr. Keate and the committee, but I hope we shall hear something soon from the corporation or from the minister on that aspect.
The question of the extension of national coverage raised by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek is very important. I listened with great interest to his remarks in committee yesterday. What he said was dealt with in part in the annual report of the corporation for 1965-66. On page 75 of that report under the heading "C.B.C. Network Expansion" we have this statement:
Each year the C.B.C. extends its network service to still more people and this year spent approximately $3,500,000 in network extension, or about 25 per cent of its capital budget.
The corporation regularly reviews its lists of communities lacking broadcast service in the light of a growing and mobile population, and estimates
Supply-C.B.C.
the costs of serving them on a priority basis, taking into account per capita costs modified by language and geographic distribution. Of the communities of 2,000 or more without television service, some 72 would tend to fall within the direct responsibility of the corporation while the C.B.C. is holding discussions with affiliates about another 34 communities and possible affiliate plans for covering them. In radio there are 78 communities of 500 or more people not receiving C.B.C. national network daytime radio service.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I confess I was reasonably satisfied with the answer given by the officials of the corporation that they did not have sufficient funds to enable them to extend coverage throughout Canada at one time. In connection with the demands for more complete coverage, the question has been asked: why go ahead with colour television before everyone is able to receive a basic radio and television service? Of course, there are other factors which must be considered-reception of colour transmissions from the United States, competition from commercial television and so on.
I am fairly impressed by the extension of television coverage which has already been achieved. In my own province, for example, there are 48 low-power transmitters for the radio network and 6 for television. I realize there are areas of British Columbia, northern Ontario and Saskatchewan, as the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek has told us, which still need service. Again, this is a matter of funds. I asked the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek in committee whether he would be prepared to vote additional moneys so that the task of extending coverage might be completed nationally and, to his credit, he said yes.
There is another matter of some importance which has to do with the corporation's budget. A confrere of the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek was questioning officials of the corporation about the time given to programs having Canadian content and to Canadian public affairs programs in the prime viewing period on television from eight o'clock to ten o'clock in the evening. The officials of the corporation said they would like to carry more but were required to derive an important part of their funds from commercial revenue. So I suggest we are faced again with the question: how much money is parliament willing to vote toward the operation of the C.B.C.?
Each year the total amount of the corporation's budget is mentioned to us, about $110 million for the current fiscal year, as though this were an outlandish sum. I do not think it

Supply-C.B.C.
is at all. My hon. friend from New Westminster put a series of questions on the order paper last year asking the cost per capita per day of the corporation's services. It amounted to about one cent per person. This is not a very large amount and I suggest it should not seem to be very much to members of parliament who are willing to acquiesce in the spending of $11 million for the repair of a pile of junk such as the Bonaventure. We are not spending a very great amount in comparison with the service we are getting. If we want additional service and want it quickly, it is up to the government to ask parliament to vote the additional money required.
One of the requests which the corporation has made over the years is that those responsible for budgeting should be able to plan ahead for periods longer than one year. This has been recommended by the committee on broadcasting and the government has stated in its white paper that it favours this idea. I believe it is a good one. However, it is the amount granted each year that will determine the extent of the service we get in this country. I do not disagree with the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek that there are parts of Canada still lacking service after all these years. But again it seems to me that the corporation is already doing good work in extending its services each year and that if we want the job done faster it is up to us to make the money available. It is up to the government to ask us to vote the necessary sums.
There are other matters connected with broadcasting to which I shall refer at this time because there will be no further opportunity this year. The Board of Broadcast Governors recently held hearings in connection with the future operation of ultra high frequency television transmission and the possible allocation of these frequencies. This is a subject of great importance. It brings us to the question of educational television programs, one which has not received, in Canada, the attention it deserves. The C.B.C. and the private stations have been devoting a certain amount of time in co-operation with the provincial authorities to the carrying of educational television broadcasting but the total time allotted to these broadcasts has been extremely limited. Space has to be found within the daily programs and the hours of transmission are not always those most convenient to the school authorities.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I suggest that we have not gone nearly far enough in Canada in using the valuable tool

of television for educational purposes. We have certainly not gone as far in its use as the United States. The future should see a great improvement in this field if we can use the ultra high frequency television band for this purpose.
In this connection a number of questions arise. Some time ago I asked the government whether it would give priority to educational outlets in the allocation of ultra high frequency television channels. As recorded at page 9362 of Hansard for Monday, October 31, the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State replied to me in part as follows:
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, and I think the hon. member will agree with me, the government will have to wait until the B.B.G. makes a ruling before it can decide on this matter. The hon. member is fully aware that the B.B.G. does not make its decisions on the spot and that sometimes we get the reports two or three weeks after the hearings.
I do not at all agree with that reply. The government has to set the frame of reference within which the B.B.G. operates, and I had hoped that in the white paper which the government issued it would have stated clearly that the educational authorities woud have prior rights when the allocation of u.h.f. channels is made. At the present time the C.B.C. is quite well served with channels, and also the private broadcasters. It is educational television which has gone short in the past and we have to rectify this situation in the future. Before a new broadcasting bill is introduced I hope this matter will be considered by the minister and that we will hear some declaration from the government that there will be priority for educational services on u.h.f. bands.
There is another matter related to this question. At a recent hearing of the B.B.G. a group headed by Kenneth Soble made an application for a third television broadcasting network in Canada. At the moment I do not want to go into the merits of whether we can afford a third network. That is quite a debatable point in itself. But this group suggested that a certain number of satellites be used, not satellite stations but satellites in air space for broadcasting purposes. They suggested two initially and perhaps four ultimately.
I want to find out more about this proposal, but at the moment I understand it is possible to have only a certain number of satellites in operation and that the United States is already using a number of them. What plans do we in Canada have to get satellites up there so that we will have a certain number that belong to us and over which we have control? If
November 23, 1966

we wait very long it seems to me the United States will pre-empt the skies and then we will have to make arrangements with that country if we want to use their satellites.
There is another question related to the use of u.h.f. channels in broadcasting. It is one which I have raised in the house a couple of times and it deals with receiving sets. I asked the government whether it had the authority to require manufacturers of television sets to include in all new sets manufactured in Canada a u.h.f. band receiver. Obviously one cannot receive u.h.f. broadcasts if one does not have a television set built for that purpose.
Two years ago the United States Congress passed a law to that effect, and at present in the United States a certain number of u.h.f. stations are in operation. It seems to me only reasonable that television set manufacturers in Canada should be required from now on to include this type of band in sets so that we will be ready for the day when u.h.f. broadcasting begins in Canada. On November 21 question No. 2,112 on the order paper, standing in my name, was answered. It read as follows:
Does the federal government, the Board of Broadcast Governors, or any other federal agency, have the power to require manufacturers of television receiving sets in Canada to include an ultra high frequency band on each unit?
The answer was no. I question this very much because I have checked some legal authorities on the matter and found that on one occasion the Privy Council made a decision that radio receiving sets come within federal jurisdiction. This decision was made in 1931 and nothing has happened since to upset it. I suggest that the government should have another look at that matter.
I wish to say one final word about the B.B.G. hearings. Parliament cannot tell the B.B.G. what to do in any particular situation. Parliament lays down certain rules but individual applications are ruled upon by the board. However, members of this house can express their views. A great many people are disturbed about one application which is before the B.B.G. at the present time. It is being made by a group of broadcasters in Barrie, Ontario, who want to relocate their broadcasting facilities closer to the Toronto area, using channel 3.
It has been said before, and my colleagues and I agree, that this type of application should not be allowed, that if there is to be an additional channel made available in the Toronto metropolitan area all persons who
Supply-C.B.C.
have made applications in the past and others should have an opportunity to apply, and that this Barrie group should not be allowed by the back door to get into the very profitable metropolitan Toronto market simply by moving a transmitter and keeping the same channel. If this were allowed it would go against any fair principle applied to the allocation of television channels.

Mr. Chairman, this year
C.B.C. will spend the fantastic sum of $113,484,000, which represents a $14 million increase apparently due to colour television being introduced across the country, particularly in the large cities, whereas certain areas are still without conventional black and white television service.
Here, in this house, we have been asking the minister for four years to extend the French television network to Victoria and Vancouver, British Columbia. After four years of repeated pleading, we have yet to witness a satisfactory step in that direction.
This will get under way in September, 1967.

In 1967, yes, but this is not yet settled.
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that the hon. minister, as well as the B.B.G. and the C.B.C., have considered the possibility of extending this service only to those French Canadian populations in British Columbia numbering between 100 and 125 thousand. This concerns the country as a whole. However, as concerns our province of Quebec, my colleague the member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) has also been urging for four years extension of the French television network to the northern region, namely Chibougamau-Chapais. And that area is still without the service. The present population of Chibougamau-Chapais is over 15,000 and the residents of those areas have to pay to be connected to a television cable; $200 for the hook-up, plus $8 a month for the use of the cable, which amounts to $96 a year, over and above the $200 installation fee.
Mr. Chairman, to my mind this is highly irregular, since the people of Chibougamau-Chapais-naturally-pay as much tax as any other Canadian citizen, contribute as much as any worker living in the Quebec, Montreal or Rouyn-Noranda area. I sincerely feel that C.B.C. could extend this service through the CKRN station in Rouyn, or through a Lac-Saint-Jean station, which would not be quite

November 23, 1966
Supply-C.B.C.
so normal, since Chibougamau-Chapais is precisely a part of Villeneuve county, according to the new electoral boundaries and is connected to the Abitibi region rather than that of Lac-Saint-Jean-Saguenay. Now, the Rouyn-Noranda station would be quite capable of broadcasting C.B.C. programs for the benefit of Chibougamau-Chapais viewers and I feel that the C.B.C. authorities could take decisions in that respect.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
If the amendment of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) to reduce the estimates by $107,942,999 is passed, there will not be much money left to pay the salaries of the president and employees of the C.B.C. The reasons why the hon. member moved his amendment are that his area is inadequately or not served at all and that very good programs have been discontinued, such as "This Hour has Seven Days" which is not shown on the French network, but was produced on the English network until last spring.
With regard to the French C.B.C. programs, we have excellent ones that are not shown however in all areas of the province. One especially which is very popular is the daily program "Aujourd'hui". Last year, that program lasted one hour daily, from Monday to Friday inclusive. This year, it was deemed advisable to cut fifteen minutes off that program, so that it only lasts three quarters of an hour, from Monday to Friday. That program "Aujourd'hui" is highly rated, but is not shown in northwestern Quebec.
Is the C.B.C. responsible for the fact that "Aujourd'hui" is not being shown over CKRN-TV, Rouyn-Noranda? If so, it seems to me that our area should enjoy good programs just as much as other areas of the province of Quebec.
I should also like to call the minister's attention to the French programs "Les affaires de 1'Etat", in which all political parties take part. We, of the Ralliement Creditiste, have been allowed a period and a half every year, that is, 13 minutes and 30 seconds on one occasion, and 6 minutes and a few seconds on another.
In my opinion, more time should be granted to programs concerning the nation's business, public administration, administration in general and Canadian politics. I do not ask here additional time only for our group but for all political parties represented in this house, so
[Mr. Caouette.l
that the population may be informed on politics in general and on economic and social affairs.
Mr. Chairman, the C.B.C. is not supposed to be concerned with politics, but I noticed many times that a great number of separatists are appearing on the national television network.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the Liberals for applauding and I would support them if they presented a motion to clean up the network, because there is socialist or separatist vermin in the C.B.C. The example which I want to give you concerns us a little.
On October 8 and 9 last, we had our national convention in Drummondville. At that time, C.B.C. cameramen and a reporter came to meet us on Saturday and, in the evening, during the eleven o'clock national news, there was about a minute and fifteen seconds of news on the occasion of our national convention. On Sunday night, there was another piece of news, but not on the national network; at six o'clock, during the Montreal local news, which does not even cover Quebec but only the area around Montreal.
That was on October 9. The following week-end the convention of Pierre Bour-gault's separatist movement was held in the province of Quebec. At that time, Mr. Chairman, for three consecutive days, on the screen of the national network which gives the news to French Canadians in western Canada as well as in the maritimes, we saw Mr. Bourgault three times when he was speaking to the people attending the convention, we were shown the hall where the delegates were meeting, we heard comments on the convention of Bourgault's separatists in the province of Quebec, and that on the whole network.
The next day I took the liberty to call the head of the news department in Montreal. For the information of those who do not know his name, I will give it. He is Mr. Frangois Peladeau, director of the C.B.C. news department in Montreal. He answered me in an arrogant manner, saying that he was the one to decide, that he did not have to take orders from members of parliament. Call him, Mr. Chairman, and you will find out about his arrogance. One would have thought that he owned the C.B.C.; it is Mr. Peladeau who decides that Mr. Bourgault will be on the air on the eleven o'clock national news and that the other parties will be completely ignored. And I think that the same unfairness prevails
November 23, 1966

against all political parties in the House of Commons.
Mr. Chairman, I must say here that, at the present time, we get much better service from the C.B.C. English network than from the French network in our province as well as throughout Canada. I am a French Canadian and I say it as such.
For much too long, we have had in Montreal people who do whatever they please in the C.B.C., who laugh at us by saying, for instance, that the government has nothing to say that parliament has nothing to say, that the C.B.C. is a crown corporation. However, it is a crown corporation which depends on credits voted by the Canadian parliament. Those people must act with justice and fairness. If Mr. Francois Peladeau of Montreal is incapable of acting fairly, he should be thrown out as soon as possible, because it is urgent.
We should put an end, Mr. Chairman, to those people inviting socialists of all shades who come here from France, Belgium, Sweden, in short from everywhere and, as soon as they land in Canada, are heard on the C.B.C. and that, when we do not even have the means or get the chance to say frankly what we think on television.
Mr. Chairman, although we vote $113 million to allow those people to impose their views on us, I do not want to impose mine on them, but I want the Canadian parliament and Canadians to be treated fairly and equitably.
Mr. Chairman, those who take an interest in Canadian politics know what happens at political conventions but surely this separatism by Mr. Bourgault does not have national scope, for it is confined within the limits of the province of Quebec. Mr. Bourgault does not believe in the rest of Canada, and the C.B.C. gives him free publicity to poison the minds of people in the province of Quebec, because Mr. Bourgault himself knows that. When you ask him the question: What is it? Is separatism a solution? He answers: No, no, it is not a solution.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Separatism is a means to go where? I do not know, but I will go anyway. There is the solution.
Is that where the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) is going?

The hon. member can think what he likes about the member for Lapointe,
Supply-C.B.C.
but I am convinced that neither the cause of the French Canadians nor the cause of the whole population of the country are thus being served. But, by this rowdy publicity, a service is rendered to separatists, who want to destroy everything in Canada and who have never built anything in their lives.
Recently, I made a speech before 800 students at the University of Sherbrooke. The C.B.C. had been invited to send representatives, but not a soul showed up. Then, a student stated that even if only good French Canadians were elected from the province of Quebec, we would still be crushed under the English majority. That is where I stated that a minority, whatever it may be, English, French, Chinese or whatever it is, that stands up and fights shall be respected anywhere in the world, but that a complacent minority shall fade away anywhere in the world.
Hear, hear.

I was then quoting Louis-Hippolyte Lafontaine who, in 1842, a few years after the uprising of 1837, worked, together with an English speaking Canadian, for the betterment of his fellow citizens and obtained for French Canadians some of the things they are still enjoying today. Lafontaine was alone. There were more people of that kind. We had some on both sides. But it is not by watching one another and fighting one against the other that Canada will grow and that Canadians will be respected. On the contrary, it is by mutual discussion on panels, without depreciating or setting aside our personal convictions, that we will promote the growth of Canada in a climate of mutual understanding of its elements. I have never seen anybody work his way up in society by crushing his neighbour. If we are unable to climb up the social or political ladder of our country by our own means, powers and skills, we do not deserve to do so, whether we are French Canadians, English speaking or Ukrainian speaking Canadians. That seems logical to me.
Returning to the C.B.C., to what extent is that so important body appreciated at the present time? Why does the C.B.C. play the game of the opponents of the Canadian people? Why are certain individuals tolerated by the authorities of the C.B.C. and even by the Department of the Secretary of State?
I understand quite well that one cannot intrude in the affairs of a crown corporation. No. But whenever there are abuses and injustices, I believe it is up to the department to

November 23, 1966
Supply-C.B.C.
interfere directly since, in the end, the department is the one having supreme control, they are the authority in the C.B.C. as well as in the B.B.G., as far as radio and television are concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to point out those facts to your attention and to that of the house, in order that injustices in the C.B.C. may be stopped. Let them stop thinking we are simple-minded. Let them respect a little the appointed authority in this country.
I come now to another field pertaining to the C.B.C., namely the national news bulletins. It is often enough quite inferior to the one seen on the English network. Once again, who looks after the preparation of those news bulletins? If it is the news service, Mr. Peladeau is again responsible. He must often be away from his office, because quite often we get international news from Viet Nam, Zambia, Rhodesia, the Belgian Congo, Belgium, France.
But nobody knows what is happening in Canada. There is no mention of Canada. For instance, a C.B.C. representative is sent to Viet Nam, to the South, to see what is going on and, at night, we hear four, five or six minutes of news dealing with Viet Nam. We are shown the killings, the war in Viet Nam.
But what is happening here in Canada, what is of interest to Canada, is forgotten, is not mentioned. What is happening in the House of Commons-you do not see a representative from the C.B.C. here, when we are discussing the $113 million we are giving them-there is not one here in the galleries even to take notes and report on the national news tonight. On the other hand, there is not one, for instance, who would be happy to see his pay cheque disappear at the end of the month. But we are not told what is happening in the country.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out to the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) the abuse over the C.B.C. French network in particular. Because that is where it happens mostly. As I said a little earlier, we are better served by the English network, and I say it as a French Canadian, than by our own French network. And I want the country to know it, and that is why I say it here in the house, and I do not care about the reactions of those people, that men like Jean Peladeau must be called to order, must be forced to act fairly-I am not saying that they should favour the Creditistes, or the Liberal party or the Conservative party, but to act as public servants of a crown

corporation, as men who are paid out of everybody's taxes. Then, we will probably get more justice.
And before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, I again ask the minister to see to it that the C.B.C. provide television coverage to the people of Chibougamau-Chapais, in northwestern Quebec. Those people need that service as much as we, in this area, and throughout Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with much of what has been said during the debate this afternoon, particularly the remarks regarding the extension of television coverage. We in this party hope that the minister in her statement will tell us something of the success of the program to establish television transmitter satellites in order to extend coverage.
My main remarks this afternoon will relate to the policy of programming. This is a subject which deserves a most careful examination by this committee because there has been little opportunity to do so. No head of the C.B.C. has been appointed yet and this makes it doubly important that we have an opportunity to examine the policy of programming of the C.B.C.
In order to examine policy I am afraid we must look at programming because, as has already been pointed out, statements of policy become absolutely meaningless when compared with the product resulting from that policy. If we have a situation in which the C.B.C. as such has no policy at the top it must be realized that there is still a policy. Much of what has happened to the C.B.C. over the past several years has beeen involved in a definite and certain policy.
Let me now refer to a couple of events we have witnessed within the last two months. First of all I wish to draw attention to the coverage given by the C.B.C. to something called "The Red China Teach-In" recently held in Toronto. The coverage of that event lasted one hour without taking into account preliminary coverage or news reports. The a.m. radio coverage lasted three hours, two of them being live, and the f.m. coverage lasted ten hours.
Let me remind hon. members just what that event was. Perhaps I can do so best by indicating the roster of speakers. At the Friday evening session the speakers were Dr. Han Suyin, a defender of the communist revolution, Lord Lindsay of Birker, chairman of the far eastern program in the School of International Service, American University,
November 23, 1966

Washington, D.C., David Crook, a teacher at the Peking Institute of Languages who has written about the early years of the revolution. The chairman was Toronto journalist and former Peking correspondent Charles Taylor.
At the third session the speakers were John Gittings, an English specialist on the Sino-Soviet split, Shinkichi Eto, associate professor of international relations at the University of Tokyo, and Stuart Schram, the U.S. born director of the Chinese and Soviet section of the Centre d'Etudes des Relations Internationales, Fondation Nationale des Sciences Politiques, Paris. The chairman was University of Toronto president Claude T. Bissell. At the final session the speakers were John Mendelson, a leftwing British Labour M.P., Leo Mates, director of the Institute of International Politics and Economy, Belgrade, and Charles Burton Marshall, professor of international relations at the John Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies. The chairman was Canadian diplomat Chester Ronning.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I wonder, when the C.B.C. was confronted with this lineup of speakers, if it gave any thought to whether in covering this event it could maintain a balance in the presentation of political thought in Canada. I have here a list of articles by a variety of authors who, regardless of their political beliefs, over and over again decry the fact that balance was not achieved in that particular series.
I tried to compare the time given to this series with the time given to another subject. I thought I could possibly obtain from the C.B.C. an indication of the time given to the NATO conference recently held in Europe, a conference at which the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska was elected president of the newly formed north Atlantic assembly. A significant change in the purpose and direction of that organization was evident and his election brought honour to this country. I submit that the activities of that organization, to which this country is committed by a solemn treaty and to which we have committed our men, our supplies and our money for a very long period of time, should have been an event of significance even to the C.B.C. So far I have been unable to obtain from them any indication that any coverage was given to the event. I trust they will be able to find that something was done on this subject by the C.B.C. because if the C.B.C.
Supply-C.B.C.
could bring Gerda from Munich they could have brought us the NATO conference from Paris.
I should also like to refer to a more recent program in which an individual named Allen Ginsberg appeared. I have obtained some material on this personality. In an extract from the Readers' Encyclopedia of American Literature there is the following:
Ginsberg claimed a predilection for apolitical mystic communism, homosexual romance, marijuana-high mentation, and cosmic ecstasy in poetry.
The 1966 Who's Who in America writes that his activities have included poetry readings in Havana, Prague, Moscow, Warsaw and London in 1965. To that glorious record we can add the C.B.C. in Toronto.
I would now like to refer to the standing committee on broadcasting which met earlier this year. At that time Mr. Haggan of the C.B.C. appeared before the committee-I know he is no longer with the corporation- and I asked him whether, if someone comes up with a really bright idea which is sensational but very much on the borderline, it can be kept off the air by people other than top management. Mr. Haggan said yes, many things are kept off the air by people other than top management. At that time I doubted that this was so and I doubt it very much more now since Mr. Ginsberg has appeared on the C.B.C. because, judging by his writings and statements, he is at the very bottom so far as morality is concerned. Nevertheless the C.B.C. put him on the air. The fact that he was given a rousing round of applause by the audience who watched him is no indication of the quality of the performer. It is merely a sad commentary on the emptiness of Canadian life at the present time.
This matter is serious. While Mr. Ginsberg was in Canada-I gather at the invitation of the C.B.C.-he also took the opportunity to recommend the use of LSD by all Canadians. I have already made reference to this matter in the last couple of days. We are involved in a battle, the most serious in which we can be involved, and I would remind the house and the official opposition that the battle is not over integration, unification or the Bona-venture but rather is for the minds of Canadians. Whoever heads the C.B.C. will be our admiral, our general and our air marshal, and may the hon. lady find a Canadian, man or woman, equal to the task.
I am reminded of a poem which I read once while sitting for an examination in English. I

November 23, 1966
Supply-C.B.C.
know examinations are no longer popular, but that is another matter.
They are still unpopular.

I know. However, occasionally they are useful, but even that is being denied now. The poem is as follows:
God is not mocked,
Hell's gates are opened
We could have kept them locked.
It had reference to world war II which had broken out partly because Canada and Canadian leadership had slept through the formative years in the 1930's.
I cannot understand why we in Canada at the present time should be so unaware of the dangers that confront us in the mass media in spite of the fact that we have in Canada a prophet who keeps reminding us about what we have created for ourselves. I am referring to Marshall McLuhan whom I have mentioned before in this house. It behooves us all to read his writings carefully. If you look at his books, "Understanding Media", you will find this reference:
All wars have been fought by the latest technology available in any culture.
He was referring to television. There is no use preparing for the enemy without if we welcome an enemy within and if we permit the minds of Canadians to be influenced by any wind that blows. We are not sufficiently discriminatory. As always, freedom is threatened on all sides. We face dangers in the world which are likely to tear it apart. We face dangers from rampant racialism which exists in many parts of the world. The C.B.C. contributed nothing to that battle when it brought Lincoln Rockwell here and gave him the use of a system of communication into which the taxpayers of this country have poured so many dollars. It did nothing to fight that enemy when it brought representatives from the Ku Klux Klan and presented them in a favourable light. It does nothing against the threat from the other side when it does not maintain a balance in programs involving a teach-in in Toronto or a person such as Mr. Ginsberg.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I should like to refer to an article on Mr. Ginsberg in Life magazine which describes his effect on some people. Mr. Ginsberg visited the city of Kansas and met students at the university. The magazine article says that "imploring faces shine with want of Allen's talk". I do not see why we should bring him

here. It is again a commentary on the emptiness of our life when he is referred to as a religious leader, as the kind of religious leader we knew on this earth thousands of years ago. In this field too we fight the wrong battles. But we do not come up to date. Although technology changes the problem so often remains the same.
Let me refer to the first story in the book of Genesis when Eve was faced with temptation. I do not happen to believe that that story is a literal record of what actually happened but it does ring with tremendous truth, and the important thing is that we get the message. The thing about Eve was that she was faced with the same subtle temptation which is now being offered to the young people of this country from many sources, and the C.B.C. is assisting in presenting this temptation through the medium of television and Mr. Ginsberg. This temptation is to opt for what is called total involvement. This is all Eve was promised, and this is what we promise through television to our young people. The effect of this involvement is just as disastrous now, and the promise is just as empty now, as it was when the idea first occurred to man.
We argue in Canada at the present time-some coverage is also given to this by the C.B.C.-that God is dead. I do not happen to believe that precept, but whether he is dead or alive alters nothing at all so far as the responsibilities of Canada's government and the management of the C.B.C. are concerned at the present time. We still have the responsibility to set a standard of moral values. If we believe that we do this with God's will and with His aid, more power to us. If there are Canadians who do not have this feeling, the responsibility is not changed one fraction. The times do not call for us to drift; they call for us to set a course.
Even Han Suyin who spoke at the teach-in knew this when she wrote her first great book that gained her the fame which ultimately brought her to the teach-in. In the preface she quoted from a poem:
The angels keep their ancient places,
Turn but a stone and start a wing 'Tis ye, 'tis your estranged faces,
That miss the many-splendored thing.
I suspect she has now forgotten the advice she gave when she found that stanza and quoted it.
I should like to call to the attention of all political parties in the house the fact that they should concern themselves with this issue.
November 23, 1966

This is a far bigger thing than politics or party. I should like to refer to an article I made mention of the other night in the Toronto Star for November 16 entitled "Why Pot Threatens Canada's New Left". The article is rather lengthy but I wish to quote briefly from it:
"Kids who are alienated and frustrated are going into the drug culture," Jack Newfield says. "When they drop out they stop going at society and become as ineffectual as the beats. A lot of people in the peace movement and the civil rights movement are getting into the drug thing. They've become disillusioned with the possibility of changing their society so now they're trying to change their own reality."
I do not see why the C.B.C. should be presenting a feature program timed, ironically enough, for a Sunday evening, which, at least up till the last program, has been built entirely around a concept gained from the use of a drug that threatens everything we hold true in Canada today. I believe that the situation is not hopeless. We echo the words of others in saying that television is something in front of which we sit, that we can concern ourselves with the direction it takes, and that we can make it a force for good in this country.
I urge all members to concern themselves very deeply with the development of both policy and program. I should like the assurance of the minister on behalf of the members of this party that the policies which are laid down are a clear expression of government thinking so that the people working in this medium of communications will clearly understand them. If they are not prepared to abide by these policies, then the C.B.C. and, if necessary, the government and parliament must be prepared to move with strength to counter the most serious threat that faces us today.

Supply-C.B.C.
she gets the opportunity to do so, whether this offer is acceptable or not.
The Fowler report also mentions the northern service.
Reference is often made to "the frozen north" or "the silent north" but, from our experience in relation to broadcasting, it would be equally apt to speak of "the forgotten north".
I believe several members who have spoken here this afternoon are in the same situation.
Out of 55 briefs submitted to the Committee, not one made any mention of the northern regions of Canada and their broadcasting needs.

Mr. Chairman, I apologize to the hon. member for interrupting his speech but I rise on a point of order. I understand there is general agreement in the committee that a vote be taken on the motion proposed this afternoon. Without going into the reasons for the agreement, may this vote be taken before six o'clock?
I agree with the comments made by the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh).

On a question of privilege, I referred a few minutes ago to the NATO conference coverage and I have received information that I did not have during the course of my remarks. I have here a communication from a Mr. Parent, supervisor, who says:
There was nothing on the NATO conference. It probably got regular news coverage, which we do not record.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. Last night in announcing the business of the house I indicated that on Thursday we would be considering the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, to be followed by consideration of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. I have been requested by the house leaders of the other parties to make a variation in that

order. Therefore the estimates to be considered tomorrow will be the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, the estimates of the Department of Finance and the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I understand further that it is the expectation that the external affairs estimates discussion will last for two hours, or until there is an opportunity for one speaker from each party to participate in the discussion, and that they will then be withdrawn from the committee if not immediately passed. estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
